faq.a: The organism forms filamentous colonies that break down connective tissue, allowing spread along fascial planes.
faq.q: Why does actinomycosis cross tissue planes?

faq.a: They are highly suggestive but not exclusive; other anaerobes can produce similar granules.
Rarely; surgery alone may remove bulk disease but recurrence is common without prolonged antibiotics.

exam: What bedside finding most strongly points to actinomycosis rather than TB? — Presence of yellow‑white sulfur granules in sinus discharge.
A patient with a cervical mass and trismus has a negative Gram stain. How do you proceed? — Obtain a biopsy for histology and culture; consider empiric penicillin if suspicion high.
When is surgical drainage indicated in actinomycosis? — When there is a large, fluctuant abscess, airway threat, or when diagnosis remains uncertain after minimally invasive sampling.
Why is penicillin preferred over doxycycline for first‑line therapy? — Penicillin is bactericidal and penetrates fibrotic tissue better; doxycycline is only bacteriostatic and used for allergy.
How does HIV infection alter management of actinomycosis? — Longer duration of antibiotics and closer monitoring for opportunistic co‑infections.
What feature on CT helps differentiate actinomycosis from malignancy? — Infiltrative mass with multiple sinus tracts and lack of a discrete enhancing tumour capsule.
Explain why a negative anaerobic culture does not rule out actinomycosis. — Actinomyces are slow‑growing and may be over‑grown by faster organisms; specimen transport and incubation are critical.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate referral to a tertiary centre? — Airway obstruction from a rapidly enlarging cervical mass.

ai.summary: Actinomycosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by Actinomyces species, presenting with indurated masses, sinus tracts and sulfur granules. It mimics malignancy and other infections, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Chronic, suppurative mass crossing tissue planes
Fistulae with yellow‑white granules
Culture: anaerobic growth, >5 days
sections.p: A slowly progressive bacterial infection caused by filamentous, anaerobic Gram‑positive Actinomyces (most often A. israelii). Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion, identification of sulfur granules, and culture or histology showing branching filaments.

t.b: Does the organism have branching Gram‑positive filaments? – Positive supports actinomycosis.
Presence of sulfur granules with filamentous filaments? – Confirms diagnosis.
Growth of Actinomyces after 5–7 days? – Confirms species.
Granulomatous inflammation with filamentous organisms? – Helps when culture unavailable.

b: Stage I: Localised mass, no fistulae
Stage II: Fistulae or sinus tracts, limited spread
Stage III: Extensive spread across fascial planes, organ involvement, or systemic sepsis
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of tissue involvement and presence of complications:

How it presents
Patients develop a painless, firm swelling that slowly enlarges, later becoming tender, with multiple sinus tracts exuding pus containing sulfur granules.
Cervicofacial: ‘lumpy jaw’, jaw swelling, trismus,Thoracic: chest wall mass, cough, haemoptysis,Abdominal: right‑lower‑quadrant mass, mimicking appendiceal tumour
sections.p: Actinomyces are normal oral, gastrointestinal and genital flora; infection follows mucosal breach.
Select tests that answer the key clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is the lesion cystic, solid or mixed? – Shows abscess cavities and sinus tracts.
What is the extent of fascial plane involvement? – Guides surgical planning.
Does the aspirate contain sulfur granules? – Provides bedside clue.
Is there leukocytosis or anaemia? – Indicates chronic infection or blood loss.
Is the patient immunosuppressed? – Influences duration of therapy.

b: Airway obstruction from cervical mass
Empyema or pleural fistula in thoracic disease
Bowel perforation, peritonitis in abdominal disease
Sepsis and distant metastatic abscesses
sections.p: Complications arise from unchecked spread or delayed treatment.

b: Penicillin G IV 2–6 weeks then oral penicillin V 6–12 months – bactericidal, penetrates fibrotic tissue
If penicillin allergy: doxycycline or macrolide – bacteriostatic, less effective
Surgical drainage of large abscesses or excision of sinus tracts – reduces bacterial load
Supportive care: analgesia, nutrition, wound care
sections.p: Long‑term high‑dose penicillin is the cornerstone; surgery is reserved for drainage, debridement or when diagnosis is uncertain.

b: Assess wound healing every 2 weeks for the first 2 months
Repeat imaging if mass does not shrink after 4 weeks of therapy
Encourage dental care, avoid prolonged oral trauma
sections.p: Monitor for clinical resolution and recurrence; educate on oral hygiene and wound care.

b: Tuberculous cold abscess – usually painless, no sulfur granules, positive AFB
Nocardiosis – filamentous but weakly Gram‑positive, acid‑fast, requires sulfonamides
Squamous cell carcinoma – firm mass, no granules, malignant cells on biopsy
sections.p: Conditions that produce similar chronic masses or sinus tracts.

b: Negative culture does not exclude disease – Actinomyces are fastidious
Granules may be missed on routine smear – need careful microscopy
CT may suggest tumour – biopsy essential before major surgery
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging findings may be non‑specific.
